claim: The default mode network (DMN) was originally termed 'task-negative' due to decreased BOLD signal during the performance of tasks requiring an external focus of attention as compared to rest.
source: The default mode network (DMN) was originally termed 'task-negative' due to decreased blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) signal ('deactivation', see Methods for full description) during the performance of tasks requiring an external focus of attention as compared to rest (Raichle, 2015; Raichle et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Raichle, 2015 and Raichle et al., 2001, which are referenced scholarly works.

claim: Processing of external stimuli increases the BOLD signal in 'task-positive' networks including the dorsal attention (DAN) and the frontoparietal network (FPN).
source: Processing of external stimuli in turn increases the BOLD signal in 'task-positive' networks including the dorsal attention (DAN) and the frontoparietal network (FPN).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about brain network responses to external stimuli.

claim: The DAN is mainly engaged when attention to sensory information is required, such as in visuo-spatial reasoning.
source: While the DAN is mainly engaged when attention to sensory information is required, such as in visuo-spatial reasoning (Fox et al., 2005), the FPN mediates cognitive control across various task conditions (Cole et al., 2013) such as the maintenance and manipulation of information also in the absence of external sensory stimuli (Scolari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fox et al., 2005.

claim: The FPN mediates cognitive control across various task conditions such as the maintenance and manipulation of information also in the absence of external sensory stimuli.
source: While the DAN is mainly engaged when attention to sensory information is required, such as in visuo-spatial reasoning (Fox et al., 2005), the FPN mediates cognitive control across various task conditions (Cole et al., 2013) such as the maintenance and manipulation of information also in the absence of external sensory stimuli (Scolari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cole et al., 2013 and Scolari et al., 2015.

claim: There is low (or anti-) correlation in BOLD signals between task-positive and default mode networks at resting-state.
source: Because of the low (or anti-) correlation in BOLD signals between task-positive and default mode networks at resting-state, it has long been assumed that an antagonism between the DMN and other large-scale networks represents a general characteristic of brain functioning (regardless if computed with or without global signal regression Buckner and DiNicola, 2019; Murphy and Fox, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as an established observation in the field, supported by citations to Buckner and DiNicola, 2019 and Murphy and Fox, 2017.

claim: The DMN can be activated during complex cognitive tasks such as memory recollection and abstract self-generated thought.
source: However, the DMN can also be activated during complex cognitive tasks (e.g., memory recollection, abstract self-generated thought; Hearne et al., 2015; Smallwood et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hearne et al., 2015 and Smallwood et al., 2021.

claim: DMN engagement during complex cognitive tasks is thought to facilitate between-network integration, instead of being a segregated network alone.
source: This DMN engagement is thought to facilitate between-network integration, instead of being a segregated network alone (Fornito et al., 2012; Leech et al., 2012; Smallwood et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fornito et al., 2012, Leech et al., 2012, and Smallwood et al., 2021.

claim: The posterior cingulate cortex (PCC)/precuneus (part of the posteromedial DMN) has been suggested to play a key role in across-network integration.
source: Moreover, some brain regions such as the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC)/precuneus (part of the posteromedial DMN) have been suggested to play a key role in across-network integration (Cocchi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cocchi et al., 2013.

claim: Task-positive attention/control networks and the DMN can flexibly switch between cooperative and antagonistic patterns to adapt to the task context at hand.
source: Thus, it has been suggested that task-positive attention/control networks and the DMN can flexibly switch between cooperative and antagonistic patterns to adapt to the task context at hand (Cocchi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cocchi et al., 2013.

claim: Our understanding of the underlying metabolic demands of context-specific neuronal processes is limited.
source: Despite these advancements in the organization of brain networks, our understanding of the underlying metabolic demands of these context-specific neuronal processes is limited (Goyal and Snyder, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goyal and Snyder, 2021.

claim: Functional PET (fPET) imaging represents a promising approach to investigate the dynamics of brain metabolism.
source: In this context, functional PET (fPET) imaging represents a promising approach to investigate the dynamics of brain metabolism.
evidence: This is stated as a general assertion about the utility of fPET imaging.

claim: fPET refers to the assessment of stimulation-induced changes in physiological processes such as glucose metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis in a single scan.
source: fPET refers to the assessment of stimulation-induced changes in physiological processes such as glucose metabolism (Hahn et al., 2016; Villien et al., 2014) and neurotransmitter synthesis (Hahn et al., 2021) in a single scan.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hahn et al., 2016, Villien et al., 2014, and Hahn et al., 2021.

claim: The temporal resolution of fPET is 6–30 s, which is considerably higher than that of a conventional bolus administration.
source: The temporal resolution of this approach of 6–30 s (Rischka et al., 2018) is considerably higher than that of a conventional bolus administration.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rischka et al., 2018.

claim: Studies using simultaneous fPET/fMRI have shown a strong spatial correspondence between the BOLD signal changes and glucose metabolism in several task-positive networks and across various tasks requiring different levels of cognitive engagement.
source: Studies using simultaneous fPET/fMRI have shown a strong spatial correspondence between the BOLD signal changes and glucose metabolism in several task-positive networks and across various tasks requiring different levels of cognitive engagement (Hahn et al., 2020; Hahn et al., 2016; Jamadar et al., 2019; Rischka et al., 2018; Stiernman et al., 2021; Villien et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Hahn et al., 2020, Hahn et al., 2016, Jamadar et al., 2019, Rischka et al., 2018, Stiernman et al., 2021, and Villien et al., 2014.

claim: Regional differences in activation patterns have been observed between BOLD and glucose metabolism in previous studies.
source: However, also regional differences in activation patterns have been observed previously between both modalities in these and previous studies (Wehrl et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wehrl et al., 2013.

claim: A dissociation between BOLD changes (negative) and glucose metabolism (positive) has been observed in the posteromedial default mode network (pmDMN) during a working memory task.
source: Moreover, a dissociation between BOLD changes (negative) and glucose metabolism (positive) has recently been observed even in the same region of the DMN during a working memory task (Stiernman et al., 2021), namely the posteromedial default mode network (pmDMN).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stiernman et al., 2021.

claim: Simple visual and motor tasks elicited a negative metabolic response in the pmDMN.
source: In contrast, simple visual and motor tasks elicited a negative metabolic response in this area (Hahn et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hahn et al., 2018.

claim: Distinct underlying metabolic processes support state-specific BOLD signal changes in the DMN.
source: These findings suggest that distinct underlying metabolic processes support state-specific BOLD signal changes in the DMN (Goyal and Snyder, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goyal and Snyder, 2021 and is inferred from the previous findings mentioned.

claim: The consistency and functional specialization of neuronal and metabolic interactions between default mode and task-positive networks is unclear.
source: However, the consistency and functional specialization of neuronal and metabolic interactions between default mode and task-positive networks is unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: It is unknown whether the observed dissociation between patterns of metabolism and BOLD changes in the DMN generalizes for complex cognitive tasks.
source: Specifically, it is unknown whether the observed dissociation between patterns of metabolism and BOLD changes in the DMN generalizes for complex cognitive tasks, and whether this in turn depends on the brain networks supporting the task performance and their interaction with the DMN.
evidence: This is stated as a research question that the study aims to address.

claim: Functional PET/MR imaging with [18F]FDG was employed during rest and performance of a visuo-spatial task requiring a broad range of cognitive functions primarily supported by the dorsal attention network.
source: To address these open questions, we employed functional PET/MR imaging with [18F]FDG during rest and performance of a visuo-spatial task requiring a broad range of cognitive functions primarily supported by the dorsal attention network (Hahn et al., 2020; Klug et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study, supported by citations to Hahn et al., 2020 and Klug et al., 2022.

claim: The results were compared to previously published data from tasks of varying complexity (working memory, eyes opening and finger tapping), primarily involving different brain networks (FPN, visual and motor, respectively).
source: The results were then compared to previously published data from tasks of varying complexity (working memory, eyes opening and finger tapping), primarily involving different brain networks (FPN, visual and motor, respectively).
evidence: This describes the comparative analysis approach used in the study.

claim: The task response of the posteromedial DMN was the main focus of interest, due to its key role in integrating specialized large-scale brain networks.
source: The task response of the posteromedial DMN was the main focus of interest, due to its key role in integrating specialized large-scale brain networks (Cocchi et al., 2013; Leech et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cocchi et al., 2013 and Leech et al., 2012.

claim: Simultaneous fPET/fMRI data and arterial blood samples were acquired from 50 healthy participants during the performance of the video game Tetris.
source: Simultaneous fPET/fMRI data and arterial blood samples were acquired from 50 healthy participants during the performance of the video game Tetris, a challenging cognitive task requiring rapid visuo-spatial processing and motor coordination (Hahn et al., 2020; Klug et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the data acquisition for the primary dataset (DS1), supported by citations to Hahn et al., 2020 and Klug et al., 2022.

claim: The Tetris task represents a challenging cognitive task requiring rapid visuo-spatial processing and motor coordination.
source: Simultaneous fPET/fMRI data and arterial blood samples were acquired from 50 healthy participants during the performance of the video game Tetris, a challenging cognitive task requiring rapid visuo-spatial processing and motor coordination (Hahn et al., 2020; Klug et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the nature of the Tetris task, supported by citations to Hahn et al., 2020 and Klug et al., 2022.

claim: The spatial overlap of negative task responses in the cerebral metabolic rate of glucose (CMRGlu) and the BOLD signal was evaluated specifically in the pmDMN.
source: From this dataset (DS1), we evaluated the spatial overlap of negative task responses in the cerebral metabolic rate of glucose (CMRGlu quantified with the Patlak plot) and the BOLD signal specifically in the pmDMN.
evidence: This describes the analysis approach used in the study.

claim: The Tetris task elicited consistent negative responses for both the BOLD signal and CMRGlu in midline core regions of the DMN, such as the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and the PCC/precuneus.
source: The Tetris task elicited consistent negative responses for both the BOLD signal and CMRGlu in midline core regions of the DMN, such as the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and the PCC/precuneus (DS1, Figure 1a, all p<0.05 FWE corrected at cluster level, high threshold of p<0.001 uncorrected).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DS1 and statistical analysis, as shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The Tetris task elicited a negative response in a cluster in the pmDMN, previously referred to as the ventral PCC.
source: This included a cluster in the pmDMN, previously referred to as the ventral PCC (Leech et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Leech et al., 2011 for the anatomical terminology.

claim: Working memory was associated with a dissociation in the DMN, where a negative BOLD response was accompanied by increased glucose metabolism in the anterior/dorsal part of the PCC.
source: In contrast, working memory was associated with a dissociation in the DMN. Here, a negative BOLD response was accompanied by increased glucose metabolism in the anterior/dorsal part of the PCC (Figure 1b; Stiernman et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a previous study (Stiernman et al., 2021) and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Tetris elicited positive changes for BOLD and CMRGlu predominantly in the visual network (VIN) and DAN.
source: Tetris elicited positive changes for BOLD and CMRGlu predominantly in the visual network (VIN) and DAN, while working memory mostly involved the FPN.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of task-induced changes across different tasks.

claim: Working memory mostly involved the FPN.
source: Tetris elicited positive changes for BOLD and CMRGlu predominantly in the visual network (VIN) and DAN, while working memory mostly involved the FPN.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the analysis of task-induced changes across different tasks.

claim: The greatest difference in positive task effects between Tetris and working memory was observed for VIN, DAN, and FPN.
source: The greatest difference in positive task effects between Tetris and working memory was therefore observed for VIN, DAN, and FPN (white bars in Figure 2c), which were selected for further evaluation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Overlapping negative responses for both imaging modalities occurred in DMN3 ('core') and DMN4 ('ventral') for Tetris, but only in DMN4 for working memory.
source: Overlapping negative responses for both imaging modalities occurred in DMN3 ('core') and DMN4 ('ventral') for Tetris, but only in DMN4 for working memory (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Simple visual stimulation (eyes open vs. eyes closed) and right finger tapping elicited increased CMRGlu in VIN and SMN (somato-motor), respectively, and a negative response mostly in DMN3.
source: Simple visual stimulation (eyes open vs. eyes closed) and right finger tapping elicited increased CMRGlu in VIN and SMN (somato-motor), respectively, and a negative response mostly in DMN3 (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DS3 and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Some of the regions with negative responses are particularly prone to susceptibility artifacts in fMRI.
source: Notably, some of the regions with negative responses are particularly prone to susceptibility artifacts in fMRI.
evidence: This is stated as a known issue in fMRI imaging.

claim: Since susceptibility artifacts are not present in fPET, the observed deactivations do not seem to be solely driven by artifacts.
source: Since this issue is not present in fPET, these deactivations do not seem to be solely driven by artifacts.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between fMRI and fPET imaging characteristics.

claim: Activations showed higher overlap between BOLD and CMRGlu (Dice coefficient Tetris = 0.57 and working memory = 0.35) than deactivations (Tetris = 0.16 and working memory = 0.06).
source: For completeness, we also evaluated the overall regional agreement between the two imaging modalities, confirming that activations (Dice coefficient Tetris = 0.57 and working memory = 0.35) showed higher overlap than deactivations (Tetris = 0.16 and working memory = 0.06; Stiernman et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of the data, with a citation to Stiernman et al., 2021.

claim: The negative CMRGlu task response in the pmDMN during Tetris significantly covaried with the positive CMRGlu response in VIN, DAN, and FPN.
source: The negative CMRGlu task response in the pmDMN during Tetris significantly covaried with the positive CMRGlu response in the other networks (Figure 3a, F = 4.84, p = 0.005).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (regression) of the experimental data, shown in Figure 3a.

claim: CMRGlu of the pmDMN was associated with that of FPN (b = 0.75, p = 0.006) and DAN (b = −0.68, p = 0.010), but not VIN (b = 0.30, p > 0.19).
source: More specifically, CMRGlu of the pmDMN was associated with that of FPN (b = 0.75, p = 0.006) and DAN (b = −0.68, p = 0.010), but not VIN (b = 0.30, p > 0.19).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (regression) of the experimental data.

claim: The influence of DAN and FPN on pmDMN was in the opposite direction.
source: Notably, the influence of DAN and FPN was in the opposite direction (as given by the opposite sign of the parameter estimates).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statistical analysis results showing opposite signs of the regression coefficients.

claim: Across individuals, the combination of low glucose metabolism in FPN and high metabolism in DAN was associated with a negative CMRGlu task response in the pmDMN.
source: That is, across individuals, the combination of low glucose metabolism in FPN and high metabolism in DAN was associated with a negative CMRGlu task response in the pmDMN.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the regression analysis results.

claim: MCM indicated that during task performance the direction of influence is from DAN (MCM z-score = 0.12 to –0.01, p = 0.005) to the pmDMN.
source: In line with the regression analysis, MCM indicated that during task performance the direction of influence is from DAN (MCM z-score = 0.12 to –0.01, p = 0.005, Figure 3b) and FPN (MCM = 0.18 vs. 0.05, p = 0.006) to the pmDMN.
evidence: The claim is supported by MCM analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: MCM indicated that during task performance the direction of influence is from FPN (MCM = 0.18 vs. 0.05, p = 0.006) to the pmDMN.
source: In line with the regression analysis, MCM indicated that during task performance the direction of influence is from DAN (MCM z-score = 0.12 to –0.01, p = 0.005, Figure 3b) and FPN (MCM = 0.18 vs. 0.05, p = 0.006) to the pmDMN.
evidence: The claim is supported by MCM analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The metabolic demands linked to pmDMN BOLD deactivations depend on the actual task at hand and the correspondingly activated functional networks (visual/motor and attention vs. control).
source: Using simultaneous PET/MR imaging, we find that the metabolic demands linked to pmDMN BOLD deactivations depend on the actual task at hand and the correspondingly activated functional networks (visual/motor and attention vs. control).
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the experimental data and analyses presented.

claim: High task-induced metabolism in the DAN but low metabolism in the FPN lead to a negative CMRGlu response in the pmDMN.
source: Specifically, we show that high task-induced metabolism in the DAN but low metabolism in the FPN lead to a negative CMRGlu response in the pmDMN.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study, supported by the regression and MCM analyses.

claim: The findings resolve the discrepancy between (non)congruent glucose demands and BOLD signal changes across different cognitive tasks.
source: These findings resolve the discrepancy between (non)congruent glucose demands and BOLD signal changes across different cognitive tasks, emphasizing the distinct metabolic underpinnings of BOLD signal deactivations during cognitive processing.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The PCC is a spatially and functionally heterogeneous region with ventral and dorsal subcomponents (vPCC/dPCC).
source: The tasks investigated in this work resulted in distinct metabolic responses in the pmDMN (Figures 1–2). This included the PCC, a spatially and functionally heterogeneous region (Leech et al., 2014) with ventral and dorsal subcomponents (vPCC/dPCC) (Vogt et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leech et al., 2014 and Vogt et al., 2006.

claim: The PCC is a central hub, connecting brain networks involved in complex behavior.
source: The PCC is a central hub, connecting brain networks involved in complex behavior (Hagmann et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hagmann et al., 2008.

claim: The PCC is thought to act as an interface between distributed functional networks by echoing their activity and tuning the balance between the internal and external focus of attention.
source: Specifically, the PCC is thought to act as an interface between distributed functional networks by echoing their activity (Leech et al., 2011) and tuning the balance between the internal and external focus of attention (Leech and Sharp, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leech et al., 2011 and Leech and Sharp, 2014.

claim: Despite a consistent negative BOLD response during external tasks, the dPCC and vPCC are differently integrated into the DMN and distinct large-scale networks underpinning task performance.
source: Despite a consistent negative BOLD response during external tasks, the dPCC and vPCC are differently integrated into the DMN and distinct large-scale networks underpinning task performance (Leech et al., 2011; Parker and Razlighi, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leech et al., 2011 and Parker and Razlighi, 2019.

claim: The dPCC and vPCC are thought to be flexibly recruited to support various cognitive functions.
source: That is, these two DMN regions are thought to be flexibly recruited to support various cognitive functions (Cocchi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cocchi et al., 2013.

claim: The vPCC is engaged in tasks with an internal focus of attention, such as autobiographical memory recollection.
source: The vPCC is engaged in tasks with an internal focus of attention (Leech and Sharp, 2014), such as autobiographical memory recollection (Svoboda et al., 2006), and when demands for externally directed attention are low (Leech et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leech and Sharp, 2014, Svoboda et al., 2006, and Leech et al., 2011.

claim: vPCC BOLD deactivation represents a downregulation of internal processing in favor of a focus on the external task as supported by DAN, VIN, and SMN.
source: Our findings add to this knowledge by suggesting that vPCC BOLD deactivation represents a downregulation of internal processing in favor of a focus on the external task for example, as supported by DAN, VIN, and SMN (Leech et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings and supported by a citation to Leech et al., 2011.

claim: A negative BOLD response paralleled by a decreased CMRGlu, as observed for Tetris as well as simple visual and motor stimulation, indicates a reduction of overall metabolism.
source: Thus, a negative BOLD response paralleled by a decreased CMRGlu, as observed for Tetris as well as simple visual and motor stimulation, indicates a reduction of overall metabolism, in line with the original understanding of DMN task-negativity (Fox et al., 2005; Hayden et al., 2009; Raichle et al., 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings and supported by citations to Fox et al., 2005, Hayden et al., 2009, and Raichle et al., 2001.

claim: The dPCC is involved in externally directed attention and plays an opposite role to the vPCC.
source: In contrast, the dPCC is involved in externally directed attention and plays an opposite role to the vPCC (Leech et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Leech et al., 2011.

claim: With increasing working memory load, the dorsal subregion exhibits stronger integration with the DMN and more pronounced BOLD signal anticorrelation with task-control networks, which is also reflected in behavioral performance.
source: With increasing working memory load, the dorsal subregion exhibits stronger integration with the DMN and more pronounced BOLD signal anticorrelation with task-control networks, which is also reflected in behavioral performance (Leech et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Leech et al., 2011.

claim: vPCC BOLD deactivation during working memory seems to reflect a metabolically expensive process that suppresses self-generated thoughts to enhance task focus, particularly when internal task demands are high.
source: Thus, vPCC BOLD deactivation during working memory seems to reflect a metabolically expensive process that suppresses self-generated thoughts to enhance task focus, particularly when internal task demands are high (Buckner and DiNicola, 2019; Hearne et al., 2015; Leech et al., 2011; Stiernman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings and supported by citations to Buckner and DiNicola, 2019, Hearne et al., 2015, Leech et al., 2011, and Stiernman et al., 2021.

claim: The distinct relationships between BOLD and CMRGlu signals that emerge during specific tasks highlight the different physiological processes contributing to neuronal activation of cognitive processing.
source: The distinct relationships between BOLD and CMRGlu signals that emerge during specific tasks highlight the different physiological processes contributing to neuronal activation of cognitive processing (Goyal and Snyder, 2021; Singh, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study's findings, supported by citations to Goyal and Snyder, 2021 and Singh, 2012.

claim: CMRGlu measured by fPET provides an absolute indicator for glucose consumption.
source: While CMRGlu measured by fPET provides an absolute indicator for glucose consumption, the BOLD signal reflects deoxyhemoglobin concentration, which depends on various factors, such as cerebral blood flow (CBF), cerebral blood volume (CBV), and the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2; Goense et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of fPET imaging.

claim: The BOLD signal reflects deoxyhemoglobin concentration, which depends on various factors, such as cerebral blood flow (CBF), cerebral blood volume (CBV), and the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2).
source: While CMRGlu measured by fPET provides an absolute indicator for glucose consumption, the BOLD signal reflects deoxyhemoglobin concentration, which depends on various factors, such as cerebral blood flow (CBF), cerebral blood volume (CBV), and the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2; Goense et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of BOLD imaging, supported by a citation to Goense et al., 2016.

claim: The BOLD signal relates to the ratio of ∆CBF/∆CMRO2.
source: In simple terms, the BOLD signal relates to the ratio of ∆CBF/∆CMRO2.
evidence: This is stated as a simplified explanation of the BOLD signal.

claim: Tasks requiring external attention and cognitive control elicit a reduction in CBF in the pmDMN.
source: Given that these types of tasks (external attention and cognitive control) elicit a reduction in CBF in the pmDMN (Shulman et al., 1997; Zou et al., 2011), CMRO2 also decreases albeit to a lesser extent (Raichle et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shulman et al., 1997 and Zou et al., 2011.

claim: CMRO2 decreases in the pmDMN during tasks requiring external attention and cognitive control, albeit to a lesser extent than CBF.
source: Given that these types of tasks (external attention and cognitive control) elicit a reduction in CBF in the pmDMN (Shulman et al., 1997; Zou et al., 2011), CMRO2 also decreases albeit to a lesser extent (Raichle et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Raichle et al., 2001.

claim: The respective metabolic processes can be described by their oxygen-to-glucose index (OGI), the ratio of CMRO2/CMRGlu.
source: Therefore, the respective metabolic processes can be described by their oxygen-to-glucose index (OGI), the ratio of CMRO2/CMRGlu.
evidence: This is stated as a definition of the OGI metric.

claim: The results suggest two distinct pathways underlying BOLD deactivations in the pmDMN that differ regarding their OGI.
source: Accordingly, our results suggest two distinct pathways underlying BOLD deactivations in the pmDMN that differ regarding their OGI.
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings.

claim: During Tetris there is a BOLD deactivation with a high OGI, resulting from a larger decrease in CMRGlu than CMRO2.
source: During Tetris there is a BOLD deactivation with a high OGI, resulting from a larger decrease in CMRGlu than CMRO2.
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings and the definition of OGI.

claim: The metabolically inactive state during Tetris is in line with electrophysiological recordings in humans and in non-human primates showing a decrease of neuronal activity in the pmDMN that covaries with the degree of exteroceptive vigilance.
source: This metabolically inactive state is in line with electrophysiological recordings in humans (Fox et al., 2018) and in non-human primates showing a decrease of neuronal activity in the pmDMN that covaries with the degree of exteroceptive vigilance (Bentley et al., 2016; Hayden et al., 2009; Shmuel et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fox et al., 2018, Bentley et al., 2016, Hayden et al., 2009, and Shmuel et al., 2006.

claim: The negative BOLD response during external tasks reflects a reduction of neuronal activity and their respective metabolic demands.
source: Therefore, we suggest that the negative BOLD response during external tasks reflects a reduction of neuronal activity and their respective metabolic demands.
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings and supported by previous electrophysiological evidence.

claim: The relatively increased CMRGlu without the corresponding surge in CMRO2 (combined with decreased CBF) hints at another kind of BOLD deactivation with a low OGI in the pmDMN during working memory, indicating energy supply by aerobic glycolysis.
source: On the other hand, the relatively increased CMRGlu without the corresponding surge in CMRO2 (combined with decreased CBF) hints at another kind of BOLD deactivation with a low OGI in the pmDMN during working memory, indicating energy supply by aerobic glycolysis (Blazey et al., 2019; Vaishnavi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings and supported by citations to Blazey et al., 2019 and Vaishnavi et al., 2010.

claim: Previous work in non-human primates has suggested a differential coupling of neuronal activity to hemodynamic oxygen supply in the PCC region.
source: Previous work in non-human primates has indeed suggested a differential coupling of neuronal activity to hemodynamic oxygen supply in this region (Bentley et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bentley et al., 2016.

claim: Tonic suppression of PCC neuronal spiking during task performance was punctuated by positive phasic responses.
source: Furthermore, tonic suppression of PCC neuronal spiking during task performance was punctuated by positive phasic responses (Hayden et al., 2009), which could indicate differences between both tasks also at the level of electrophysiologically measured activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hayden et al., 2009.

claim: One of the current hypotheses regarding BOLD deactivations proposes that CMRO2 and CBF are affected by the balance of the excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters, specifically GABA and glutamate.
source: On the neurotransmitter level, one of the current hypotheses regarding BOLD deactivations proposes that CMRO2 and CBF are affected by the balance of the excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters, specifically GABA and glutamate (Buzsáki et al., 2007; Lauritzen et al., 2012; Sten et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buzsáki et al., 2007, Lauritzen et al., 2012, and Sten et al., 2017.

claim: In the PCC, glutamate release prevents negative BOLD responses.
source: In the PCC, glutamate release prevents negative BOLD responses (Hu et al., 2013), whereas a lower glutamate/GABA ratio is associated with greater deactivation (Gu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hu et al., 2013.

claim: A lower glutamate/GABA ratio is associated with greater deactivation in the PCC.
source: In the PCC, glutamate release prevents negative BOLD responses (Hu et al., 2013), whereas a lower glutamate/GABA ratio is associated with greater deactivation (Gu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gu et al., 2019.

claim: Glutamate elicits proportional glucose consumption.
source: As glutamate elicits proportional glucose consumption (Lundgaard et al., 2015; Zimmer et al., 2017), decreases in glutamate signaling in the pmDMN could indeed explain both, the decreased BOLD response and decreased CMRGlu during the Tetris task.
